title: Looking a word up in a dictionary
description: A dictionary stores definitions that are looked up by word. Implement a function called NewDictionary that receives nothing and returns a collection of definitions keyed by word, holding exactly two entries: the word "test" defined as "this is just a test", and the word "map" defined as "a collection of key/value pairs". Implement a function called Search that receives such a collection along with a word, and returns the definition stored under that word: Search([test: this is just a test], "test") -> "this is just a test". Nothing is stored under a word the collection does not define, so looking one up gives back empty text rather than failing: Search([test: this is just a test], "unknown") -> "".
objective: Practice declaring a collection of key/value pairs and reading a value out of it by key.

title: Telling a missing entry apart from a zero
description: A scoreboard records the points each player scored, keyed by player name. A player can legitimately have scored zero, and a player who never played has no entry at all; the two must be distinguishable. Implement a function called Score that receives a scoreboard along with a player name and returns two things: the points recorded for that player, and whether the scoreboard has an entry for them at all. For a scoreboard holding [chris: 33, ruth: 0]: Score(scoreboard, "chris") -> 33, true. Score(scoreboard, "ruth") -> 0, true, because ruth really did score zero. Score(scoreboard, "nobody") -> 0, false, because there is no entry for nobody at all.
objective: Practice reading a key/value collection in the form that also reports whether the key was there, so a missing entry is not mistaken for a stored zero.

title: A named type that is a failure value
description: Looking a word up can fail, and callers should be able to check exactly which failure came back instead of matching on its message text. Declare a named type called DictionaryErr built on the text type, and make it usable as a failure value by giving it a method called Error that returns the text it holds. Because the type is built on text, a fixed failure can be exposed as a constant rather than built at start-up: declare one called ErrNotFound whose message reads exactly "could not find the word you were looking for". Implement a function called Search that receives a collection of definitions keyed by word along with a word, and returns the definition together with a failure. A word that has a definition gives that definition back and reports nothing wrong: Search([test: this is just a test], "test") -> "this is just a test", no failure. A word with no definition gives back empty text and reports ErrNotFound itself, rather than a freshly built failure that merely carries the same message: Search([test: this is just a test], "unknown") -> "", ErrNotFound.
objective: Practice turning a named type over text into a failure value, and exposing a fixed failure callers can compare against directly.

title: Adding and removing entries in place
description: Declare a named type called Dictionary built on a collection of definitions keyed by word. A dictionary handed to another part of the program and modified there has to show those modifications to everyone else holding it, without the caller having to hand over a pointer. Also declare a named type called DictionaryErr built on the text type with a method called Error that returns the text it holds, and expose a failure called ErrNotFound whose message reads exactly "could not find the word you were looking for". Give Dictionary three methods. Search receives a word and returns its definition plus a failure: a defined word gives its definition and nothing wrong, an undefined word gives empty text and ErrNotFound. Add receives a word and a definition and stores it, replacing any definition already held for that word. Delete receives a word and removes its definition; deleting a word that has no definition changes nothing and is not a failure. Starting from a dictionary holding [test: this is just a test]: Add("map", "a collection") then Search("map") -> "a collection". Add("test", "a replacement") then Search("test") -> "a replacement". Delete("test") then Search("test") -> ErrNotFound.
objective: Practice writing methods that modify the key/value collection they were called on, which they can do without a pointer receiver.

title: Branching on which failure came back
description: Declare a named type called Dictionary built on a collection of definitions keyed by word, along with a named type called DictionaryErr built on the text type with a method called Error that returns the text it holds, so failures can be exposed as constants. Expose two of them: ErrNotFound, reading exactly "could not find the word you were looking for", and ErrWordExists, reading exactly "cannot add word because it already exists". Give Dictionary a method called Search that receives a word and returns its definition plus a failure: a defined word gives its definition and nothing wrong, an undefined word gives empty text and ErrNotFound. Then give it two more methods that each decide what to do purely from what Search reported back, treating the case where Search reported nothing wrong as one of the outcomes to branch on. Add receives a word and a definition and returns a failure: a word with no definition yet gets it stored and nothing is reported wrong; a word that already has a definition keeps it exactly as it was and Add reports ErrWordExists. Update receives a word and a definition and returns a failure: a word that already has a definition gets it replaced and nothing is reported wrong; a word with no definition yet gets nothing stored at all and Update reports ErrNotFound. Starting from a dictionary holding [test: this is just a test]: Add("map", "a collection") -> no failure, then Search("map") -> "a collection". Add("test", "something else") -> ErrWordExists, then Search("test") -> "this is just a test", unchanged. Update("test", "a replacement") -> no failure, then Search("test") -> "a replacement". Update("map", "a collection") on a dictionary with no entry for map -> ErrNotFound, then Search("map") -> ErrNotFound, because nothing was stored.
objective: Practice driving a decision from which failure an operation reported back, with no failure at all being one of the cases handled.
